learn.hook: Mumbai at 32°C feels far stickier than Jaipur at 38°C. The difference is the water vapour in the air.
points: Water vapour in the air varies from zero to four per cent by volume of the atmosphere. Water moves continuously between the atmosphere, oceans and continents through evaporation, transpiration, condensation and precipitation.
Water vapour present in the air is called humidity.
Absolute humidity is the actual amount of water vapour present: the weight of water vapour per unit volume of air, expressed in grams per cubic metre. It differs from place to place.
The ability of air to hold water vapour depends entirely on its temperature.

Relative humidity is the percentage of moisture present in the atmosphere compared with its full capacity at a given temperature. RH = (actual vapour ÷ capacity at that temperature) × 100. When temperature changes, the capacity changes, so relative humidity changes.

example.q: Air at 30°C can hold 30 g/m³ of water vapour but actually holds 18 g/m³. Find its absolute and relative humidity.
steps: Absolute humidity = actual vapour = 18 g/m³.
Relative humidity = 18 ÷ 30 × 100.

learn.reallife: Weather apps show relative humidity because it tells you how close the air is to saturation, which is why 80% RH in Chennai feels so muggy.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's the difference between absolute and relative humidity?'
teach.praise: Absolute humidity is the actual grams of vapour, relative humidity the percentage of capacity, which depends on temperature. Gappu is no longer sweating it!
teach.nudge: Define absolute and relative humidity and explain the role of temperature.

learn.hook: On a hot day a glass of cold water 'sweats'. The air touching it has cooled to its dew point.
points: Air holding moisture to its full capacity at a given temperature is saturated: it cannot hold any more water vapour at that temperature.
The temperature at which saturation occurs in a given sample of air is its dew point.
Relative humidity is greater over the oceans and least over the continents.
Evaporation is the process by which water changes from liquid to gas. Heat is the main cause; the heat absorbed in this change is the latent heat of vaporisation.

Evaporation increases with (i) higher temperature, which raises the air's capacity to hold moisture, (ii) low moisture content (unsaturated air can absorb more), and (iii) air movement, which replaces the saturated layer with unsaturated air.

example.q: Why do clothes dry faster on a hot, dry, windy day than on a humid, still day?
steps: High temperature increases the air's capacity to hold vapour.
Dry (unsaturated) air can absorb more moisture.
Wind replaces the moist layer next to the clothes with drier air.
All three increase evaporation.
example.answer: Because high temperature, dry air and wind all speed up evaporation.

learn.reallife: Salt pans in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu rely on hot sun and dry winds to evaporate sea water and leave salt behind.

learn.hook: Every raindrop starts as invisible vapour clinging to a speck of dust, salt or smoke.
points: Condensation is the transformation of water vapour into water. It is caused by loss of heat. When moist air cools to the point where it can no longer hold its vapour, the excess condenses.
If vapour changes directly into the solid form (ice), it is called sublimation.

In free air, condensation occurs around very small particles called hygroscopic condensation nuclei: dust, smoke and salt from the ocean are good nuclei because they absorb water. Condensation also occurs when moist air touches a colder object, or when the temperature is close to the dew point.

Condensation takes place: (i) when air temperature is reduced to the dew point with volume constant; (ii) when both volume and temperature are reduced; (iii) when moisture is added through evaporation. The most favourable condition is a decrease in air temperature.
Condensation depends on the amount of cooling and the relative humidity. After condensation, moisture takes the form of dew, frost, fog or clouds, depending on temperature and location.

example.q: Identify the process: (a) water vapour forming droplets around salt particles over the Arabian Sea; (b) water vapour turning straight into ice crystals on a freezing night.
steps: (a) Vapour → liquid droplets around nuclei → condensation.
(b) Vapour → solid ice directly, skipping the liquid → sublimation.

learn.reallife: Delhi's winter smog becomes thicker fog partly because pollution particles act as plentiful condensation nuclei.

topics.title: Forms of condensation: dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds

learn.hook: Winter mornings in Punjab bring fog so thick that trains run hours late. Up in Shimla, the same chill leaves sparkling frost on rooftops.
points: Dew: moisture deposited as water droplets on cooler surfaces of solid objects (stones, grass blades, leaves) rather than on nuclei in the air. Ideal conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, and cold, long nights. The dew point must be above the freezing point.

Frost: forms on cold surfaces when condensation takes place below freezing point (0°C), i.e., when the dew point is at or below freezing. Excess moisture is deposited as minute ice crystals. Conditions for white frost are the same as for dew, except the air temperature must be at or below freezing.

Fog: when the temperature of an air mass with much water vapour falls suddenly, condensation takes place within it on fine dust particles. Fog is a cloud with its base at or very near the ground; visibility becomes poor to zero. Fog mixed with smoke in urban and industrial areas is smog.

Mist contains more moisture than fog (each nucleus has a thicker layer of moisture). Mists are frequent over mountains where rising warm air meets cold surfaces; fogs are drier and occur where warm air currents meet cold currents.
Clouds are masses of minute water droplets or tiny ice crystals formed by condensation of water vapour in free air at considerable elevations.

example.q: On a clear, calm, cold night, the dew point is 3°C. Will dew or frost form, and why?
steps: Dew forms when the dew point is above freezing (0°C).
Frost forms when the dew point is at or below freezing.
Here the dew point is 3°C, above 0°C.
So dew will form.
example.answer: Dew, because the dew point (3°C) is above freezing.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways runs anti-fog devices on locomotives in the Indo-Gangetic plain every winter because dense fog cuts visibility to near zero.

learn.hook: Wispy white streaks high in a blue sky, cotton-wool puffs on a summer afternoon, a dark grey blanket before the monsoon burst: each tells you something about the weather.
points: Clouds are grouped by their height, expanse, density and transparency or opaqueness into four basic types: cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus.
Cirrus: formed at high altitudes (8,000–12,000 m); thin, detached and feathery; always white.
Cumulus: look like cotton wool; generally formed at 4,000–7,000 m; exist in scattered patches with a flat base.

Stratus: layered clouds covering large portions of the sky, formed by loss of heat or mixing of air masses with different temperatures. Nimbus: black or dark grey, formed at middle levels or very near the surface; extremely dense and opaque to the sun's rays; shapeless masses of thick vapour, sometimes so low they seem to touch the ground.

Combinations: high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus); middle clouds (altostratus, altocumulus); low clouds (stratocumulus, nimbostratus); clouds with extensive vertical development (cumulus, cumulonimbus).

example.q: Identify the cloud: thin, white and feathery at about 10,000 m.
steps: High altitude (8,000–12,000 m) → high cloud.
Thin, detached, feathery and white.
These match cirrus.

learn.reallife: Pilots and IMD observers note cumulonimbus clouds carefully, as they bring thunderstorms and turbulence to flights over India.

topics.title: Precipitation: rain, snow, sleet and hail

learn.hook: Cut a hailstone in half and you will see rings like an onion, a record of its trips up and down inside a storm cloud.
points: Continuous condensation in free air makes condensed particles grow. When air resistance can no longer hold them against gravity, they fall to the earth. This release of moisture after condensation is precipitation; it can be liquid or solid.

Precipitation in the form of water is rainfall. When the temperature is lower than 0°C, precipitation takes place as fine flakes of snow (snowfall); moisture is released as hexagonal crystals that form snowflakes.

Sleet is frozen raindrops and refrozen melted snow-water. It occurs when a layer of air above freezing overlies a sub-freezing layer near the ground: raindrops leaving the warmer air solidify in the colder air and reach the ground as small ice pellets, not bigger than the raindrops.

Hailstones are rain drops that, after being released by the clouds, solidify into small rounded pieces of ice while passing through colder layers. They have several concentric layers of ice, one over the other.
Sleet and hail are limited in occurrence and sporadic in both time and space.

example.q: Rain falls from a warm layer of air into a freezing layer near the ground and reaches the surface as small ice pellets the size of raindrops. What is this?
steps: A warm layer over a sub-freezing layer near the ground.
Raindrops freeze in the cold layer.
Ice pellets no bigger than the raindrops reach the ground.
This is sleet.

learn.reallife: Hailstorms in March and April damage wheat and mustard crops in Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh, and farmers can claim insurance under crop insurance schemes.

learn.hook: Mangaluru gets over 300 cm of rain a year, but Bengaluru, not far east, gets only about 100 cm. The Western Ghats stand in between.
points: On the basis of origin, rainfall is of three main types: convectional, orographic (relief) and cyclonic (frontal).

Convectional rain: heated air becomes light and rises in convection currents; it expands, loses heat and condenses into cumulus clouds. Heavy rain with thunder and lightning falls but does not last long. It is common in summer or the hotter part of the day, in equatorial regions and interior parts of continents, especially in the Northern Hemisphere.
Orographic (relief) rain: a saturated air mass meeting a mountain is forced to rise; it expands, cools and its moisture condenses. The windward slopes receive greater rainfall.

After crossing the mountain, the air descends the leeward slope and warms up, increasing its capacity to hold moisture, so leeward slopes remain dry. The area on the leeward side that gets less rain is the rain-shadow area. A diagram of a mountain with rainy windward and dry leeward slopes shows this.
Cyclonic (frontal) rain is associated with cyclones and fronts, as studied in the chapter on atmospheric circulation and weather systems.

example.q: Explain why Mumbai gets heavy monsoon rain while Pune, east of the Western Ghats, gets much less.
steps: South-west monsoon winds blow from the Arabian Sea towards the Western Ghats.
They rise up the windward (western) slopes, cool and give heavy orographic rain to Mumbai and the Konkan.
After crossing the Ghats, the air descends and warms on the leeward side.
Pune lies in this rain-shadow area, so it gets less rain.
example.answer: Mumbai is on the windward side (orographic rain); Pune lies in the rain shadow.

learn.reallife: Agumbe in Karnataka, on the windward Ghats, gets very heavy rain, while districts like Chitradurga in the rain shadow are drought-prone.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does it rain more on one side of a mountain than the other? What other kinds of rain are there?'
teach.praise: Convectional from heating, orographic over mountains with a rain shadow, and cyclonic along fronts. Gappu is soaked in knowledge!
teach.nudge: Name the three types of rainfall and explain the rain-shadow effect.

learn.hook: Why does western Europe get rain all year, while eastern coasts in the 35°–40° belt get heavier rain than western ones? Latitude, winds and mountains decide.
points: In general, rainfall decreases steadily from the equator towards the poles.
Coastal areas receive more rain than the interiors of continents. Rainfall is more over the oceans than over landmasses, because oceans are great sources of water.
Between 35° and 40° N and S, rain is heavier on the eastern coasts and decreases towards the west.
Between 45° and 65° N and S, due to the westerlies, rainfall is first received on the western margins of continents and decreases towards the east.
Wherever mountains run parallel to the coast, rain is greater on the coastal plain on the windward side and decreases towards the leeward side.

example.q: A continent at 55°N gets rain-bearing westerlies. Which coast will be wetter, and why?
steps: Between 45° and 65° N, the westerlies blow from the west.
They bring moisture from the ocean first to the western margin.
Rainfall decreases eastwards into the interior.
So the western coast is wetter.
example.answer: The western coast, because the westerlies bring rain to the western margins first.

learn.reallife: India's own pattern mirrors these rules: the windward Western Ghats and the north-east (with mountains facing moist winds) are wet, while interior Rajasthan is dry.

quiz.q: Between 45° and 65° N and S, rainfall is first received on the:
quiz.explain: The westerlies bring moisture to western margins first.

quiz.q: Between 35° and 40° N and S of the equator, rain is heavier on:
quiz.explain: NCERT notes heavier rain on eastern coasts in this belt.

quiz.q: Rainfall is more over oceans than over landmasses because:
options: Oceans are great sources of water
Land is closer to the sun
quiz.explain: Abundant evaporation over oceans supplies moisture.

quiz.q: Where mountains run parallel to a coast, rainfall is greatest:
options: On the mountain's far interior side
quiz.explain: Moist winds rise against the mountains on the windward side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the leeward side is wettest

quiz.q: Compared with the interior of continents, coastal areas generally receive:
quiz.explain: Coasts are closer to moisture sources.

quiz.q: The westerlies influence rainfall mainly between which latitudes?
quiz.explain: NCERT links the westerlies with 45°–65° N and S.
quiz.mistake: Places the westerlies in the tropics

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Western Europe gets rainfall throughout the year.
Reason (R): It lies in the westerly belt, where western margins of continents receive rain first.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Moist westerlies from the Atlantic bring rain to western Europe year-round.
quiz.mistake: Thinks western Europe has a monsoon

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Which parts of the world get the most rain, and why?'
teach.praise: Wetter at the equator, on coasts, on western margins in the westerly belt and on windward slopes. Gappu has mapped the rain!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the main patterns of world rainfall distribution.

learn.hook: Two places can both get 100 cm of rain a year, yet one is lush and one is parched. When the rain falls matters as much as how much.
points: Over 200 cm per year: the equatorial belt, the windward slopes of mountains along the western coasts in the cool temperate zone, and the coastal areas of the monsoon lands.
100–200 cm per year: interior continental areas (moderate rainfall); coastal areas of continents also receive moderate amounts.
50–100 cm per year: the central parts of tropical lands and the eastern and interior parts of temperate lands.
Less than 50 cm per year: areas in the rain-shadow zone of the interiors of continents and high latitudes.

Seasonal distribution matters for effectiveness. In the equatorial belt and western parts of cool temperate regions, rain is distributed evenly through the year; monsoon lands get most rain in summer; Mediterranean lands get rain mainly in winter. Exam tip: practise absolute vs relative humidity, forms of condensation, types of rainfall with diagrams, and reading world rainfall maps.

example.q: Classify the rainfall regime: (a) Konkan coast of India, about 250 cm; (b) a rain-shadow interior plateau, about 40 cm.
steps: (a) Over 200 cm and a coastal monsoon land → heavy rainfall regime (over 200 cm).
(b) Less than 50 cm in a rain-shadow interior → very low rainfall regime.
example.answer: (a) Over 200 cm (heavy); (b) Less than 50 cm (very low).

learn.reallife: Indian agriculture depends on the summer monsoon season, which brings most of the country's annual rainfall in June to September.

quiz.q: Which region receives over 200 cm of rainfall per annum?
quiz.explain: The equatorial belt, windward western coasts of cool temperate zones and monsoon coasts get over 200 cm.

quiz.q: Areas in the rain-shadow zone of the interiors of continents and high latitudes receive:
quiz.explain: These are the driest regimes.

quiz.q: The central parts of tropical lands and the eastern and interior parts of temperate lands receive:
quiz.explain: NCERT puts these in the 50–100 cm regime.
quiz.mistake: Places them in a wetter category

quiz.q: Interior continental areas generally receive moderate rainfall of:
quiz.explain: NCERT gives 100–200 cm for interior continental areas.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the drier interior rain-shadow zones

quiz.q: In which region is rainfall distributed evenly throughout the year?
quiz.explain: The equatorial belt gets rain in all seasons.
quiz.mistake: Thinks monsoon lands get year-round rain

quiz.q: Mediterranean lands receive most of their rainfall in:
quiz.explain: Mediterranean climates have dry summers and rainy winters.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Mediterranean rain comes in summer like the monsoon

quiz.q: Why is the seasonal distribution of rainfall important?
options: It decides how effective the rainfall is for crops and water supply
quiz.explain: Even good totals are less useful if all rain falls in a short season.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only the annual total matters

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Coastal areas of monsoon lands receive heavy rainfall of over 200 cm.
Reason (R): Moist monsoon winds from the oceans bring heavy rain to these coasts in summer.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Onshore monsoon winds deliver large amounts of moisture to coastal areas.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Which places get lots of rain and which get little? Does the season matter?'
teach.praise: Over 200 cm at the equator and monsoon coasts, under 50 cm in rain shadows and high latitudes, and seasons matter too! Gappu is weather-wise.
teach.nudge: Describe the rainfall regimes and the seasonal patterns.
